title: Chromosomes and Meiosis: The Physical Basis of Mendel's Laws

generated.pipeline: extract → Opus draft → Sonnet accuracy gate → Sonnet fixes

cards.front: In a normal meiosis, what does meiosis I separate, and what does meiosis II separate?
cards.back: Meiosis I deals one homolog of every pair to each daughter cell. Meiosis II splits sister chromatids, the two copies made of each chromosome before meiosis began.
cards.why: Saying that meiosis I separates sisters is the commonest exam error.
cards.quote: Meiosis II then splits sisters, the two copies made of each chromosome before meiosis began.

cards.front: Which event in meiosis gives Mendel's law of segregation, and which gives independent assortment?
cards.back: Segregation: the deal of homologs apart at anaphase I, so each gamete gets one allele of each gene. Independent assortment: each pair's own random orientation (a fair coin toss) at metaphase I.
cards.quote: The deal gives the law of segregation: each gamete gets one allele of each gene, so an Aa cell gives two A and two a.

cards.front: {{c1::Homologous chromosomes}} are the two members of a pair, one inherited from each parent, carrying the same genes at the same loci but possibly different alleles.
cards.back: Homologs: the left and right shoe of a pair.
cards.quote: the two members of a pair, one inherited from each parent
cards.section: Count before you divide: homologs, sisters and ploidy

cards.front: {{c1::Sister chromatids}} are the two identical copies of one chromosome made in S phase, still joined at the centromere.
cards.back: A shoe and its stapled copy.
cards.quote: the two identical copies of one chromosome made in S phase
cards.section: Count before you divide: homologs, sisters and ploidy

cards.front: How do you count chromosomes in a cell whose chromosomes have replicated?
cards.back: Count centromeres, not arms. A replicated chromosome, two sister chromatids joined at a centromere, is still one chromosome.
cards.quote: The rule that saves most students on exams: count centromeres, not arms.
cards.section: Count before you divide: homologs, sisters and ploidy

cards.front: {{c1::Ploidy}} is the number of complete chromosome sets in a cell: one set is haploid (n), two sets diploid (2n).
cards.quote: Ploidy is the number of complete chromosome sets in a cell.
cards.section: Count before you divide: homologs, sisters and ploidy

cards.front: What does 1C mean, and what is the C value of a diploid cell in G1 and after S phase?
cards.back: 1C is the DNA content of one unreplicated haploid set. A diploid cell is 2C in G1 and 4C after S phase.
cards.quote: One unreplicated haploid set, one shoe of each pair with nothing stapled on, is 1C.
cards.section: Count before you divide: homologs, sisters and ploidy

cards.front: Why can a cell's ploidy and its C value disagree? Give the fruit fly example after S phase.
cards.back: Ploidy counts chromosome sets (centromeres); C counts DNA. After S phase a fly cell holds 8 chromosomes but 16 chromatids and 4C of DNA, and is still diploid.
cards.quote: They can disagree: after S phase a fly cell holds 16 chromatids and 4C of DNA, and is still diploid.
cards.section: Count before you divide: homologs, sisters and ploidy

cards.front: In prophase I, a synapsed pair of homologs, two homologs and four chromatids, is called a {{c1::bivalent}} (also a tetrad).
cards.back: The pairing itself is synapsis.
cards.quote: That pairing is synapsis, and a synapsed pair is a bivalent: two homologs, four chromatids (exams also call it a tetrad).
cards.section: Meiosis I separates homologs; meiosis II separates sisters

cards.front: What is crossing over, between which chromatids does it occur, and in which stage?
cards.back: Exchange of segments between non-sister chromatids (chromatids of different homologs) while homologs are paired, in prophase I.
cards.quote: While paired, homologs can exchange segments between non-sister chromatids (chromatids of different homologs), which is crossing over
cards.section: Meiosis I separates homologs; meiosis II separates sisters

cards.front: Contrast mitosis and meiosis in pairing and outcome.
cards.back: In mitosis homologs do not synapse; each chromosome lines up alone, sisters part, and both daughters keep two sets. Meiosis pairs homologs, halves the sets and shuffles them.
cards.quote: Mitosis differs at the very first step: homologs do not synapse or form bivalents.
cards.section: Meiosis I separates homologs; meiosis II separates sisters

cards.front: In a fruit fly (2n = 8), how many separate units line up across the spindle at mitotic metaphase, and how many at metaphase I of meiosis?
cards.back: Mitosis: 8, each replicated chromosome lining up alone. Metaphase I: 4 bivalents, each a pair of homologs facing opposite poles.
cards.why: Homologs synapse into bivalents only in meiosis; in mitosis they never pair.
cards.quote: Each chromosome lines up alone and its sisters part, so both daughter cells keep the parent's two sets.
cards.section: Meiosis I separates homologs; meiosis II separates sisters

cards.front: A diploid organism has 2n = 14. Give chromosomes, chromatids, bivalents and C value for one cell in prophase I, after meiosis I, and after meiosis II.
cards.back: Prophase I: 14 chromosomes, 28 chromatids, 7 bivalents, 4C. After meiosis I: 7, 14, 0, 2C. After meiosis II: 7, 7, 0, 1C.
cards.why: S phase doubles chromatids and DNA, not chromosomes; anaphase I halves chromosomes; anaphase II halves chromatids.
cards.quote: Step 1. S phase doubles chromatids and DNA but not chromosomes: 8 chromosomes, 8 × 2 = 16 chromatids, 4C.
cards.section: Meiosis I separates homologs; meiosis II separates sisters

cards.front: Why is a cell just after meiosis I haploid yet still 2C?
cards.back: It has one centromere from each pair, so one set: haploid. But each chromosome still has two chromatids, so its DNA equals a diploid cell in G1, 2C.
cards.quote: Each chromosome still has two chromatids, so its DNA content is 2C, the same as a diploid cell in G1.
cards.section: Meiosis I separates homologs; meiosis II separates sisters

cards.front: In an organism with 2n = 20, a cell holds 10 chromosomes, each made of two chromatids. Where is it in meiosis, is it haploid or diploid, and what is its C value?
cards.back: Between meiosis I and anaphase II; haploid (one set of 10 centromeres); 2C, because each chromosome still has two chromatids.
cards.quote: Four centromeres, one from each pair: the cell is haploid, one set.
cards.section: Meiosis I separates homologs; meiosis II separates sisters

cards.front: DNA content is measured in single cells from a testis, with mature sperm set at 1C. Cells fall into 1C, 2C and 4C classes. Which cells can be in each class, and how would you split the 2C class?
cards.back: 1C: haploid cells after meiosis II. 2C: diploid cells in G1, plus cells after meiosis I. 4C: diploid cells after S phase, including those in prophase I. Count chromosomes: 46 single-chromatid versus 23 two-chromatid.
cards.why: C counts DNA, not sets, so a haploid cell with replicated chromosomes and a diploid G1 cell share 2C.
cards.quote: The C value counts DNA instead of centromeres.
cards.section: Count before you divide: homologs, sisters and ploidy

cards.front: Trace an Aa locus through meiosis. Why do exactly two of the four products carry A?
cards.back: After S phase one homolog carries A on both sisters, the other a on both. Anaphase I sends A and a to different cells; anaphase II splits identical sisters.
cards.quote: Anaphase I separates the homologs, so A and a go to different cells; anaphase II separates identical sisters.
cards.section: Where Mendel's laws live in the cell

cards.front: An Aa cell skips meiosis I and runs only meiosis II. What do its products carry, and how many chromosome sets?
cards.back: Each product is Aa, with two sets like its parent. Anaphase II gives each product one chromatid of every chromosome, from both homologs: a mitosis-like division, no reduction.
cards.why: Segregation needs meiosis I, the step that deals homologs apart.
cards.quote: Segregation needs meiosis I, the step that deals homologs apart.
cards.section: Where Mendel's laws live in the cell

cards.front: What physical event at metaphase I produces independent assortment?
cards.back: Each bivalent can face the spindle two ways, like a coin toss, independently of the other pairs.
cards.quote: Each bivalent can face the spindle two ways, like a coin toss, independently of the other pairs.
cards.section: Where Mendel's laws live in the cell

cards.front: A diploid species has 2n = 10. Ignoring crossing over, how many chromosome combinations can its gametes carry, and what fraction carry only chromosomes inherited from the mother?
cards.back: n = 5 pairs, each oriented two ways: 2^5 = 32 combinations. All-maternal is one of them: (1/2)^5 = 1/32.
cards.why: Use 2 raised to the number of pairs, not the chromosome count.
cards.quote: 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 2^4 = 16 possible chromosome combinations in a gamete
cards.section: Where Mendel's laws live in the cell

cards.front: Ignoring crossing over, how many chromosome combinations can a human gamete carry, and is the real variety larger or smaller?
cards.back: n = 23: 2^23 = 8,388,608, about 8.4 million. Real variety is larger, because the count ignores crossing over.
cards.quote: For humans, 2n = 46 and n = 23: 2^23 = 8,388,608, about 8.4 million
cards.section: Where Mendel's laws live in the cell

cards.front: A fly is Aa Bb, loci on different chromosomes, no crossing over. Why does one meiosis give only two kinds of gamete, yet the fly's gametes show AB, Ab, aB and ab at 1/4 each?
cards.back: One meiosis takes one orientation: 2 AB + 2 ab or 2 Ab + 2 aB. The two orientations are equally likely, so over many meioses each class is 1/4.
cards.quote: Mendel's four equal classes belong to the gametes of many meioses.
cards.section: Where Mendel's laws live in the cell

cards.front: For which pairs of loci does independent assortment hold, and when does it fail?
cards.back: It holds for loci on different chromosomes, or far apart on one. Loci close together on one chromosome tend to travel together: linkage.
cards.quote: Loci close together on one chromosome tend to travel together: linkage and mapping.
cards.section: Where Mendel's laws live in the cell

cards.front: In animals, how do the products of one meiosis differ in sperm production and egg production?
cards.back: Sperm: four haploid cells, all becoming sperm. Egg: unequal divisions give one large egg and small polar bodies that do not become gametes.
cards.quote: In sperm production, one meiosis gives four haploid cells and all four become sperm.
cards.section: Four sperm, one egg

cards.front: In mammals, when does the egg finish meiosis II?
cards.back: Only after a sperm enters.
cards.quote: in mammals the egg finishes meiosis II only after a sperm enters
cards.section: Four sperm, one egg

cards.front: A woman is Aa. One of her eggs carries a, and no crossover fell between the locus and its centromere. What did the first polar body receive, and what did the second polar body receive?
cards.back: First polar body: the A homolog, as two A chromatids. Second polar body: one a chromatid, the sister of the egg's a.
cards.why: Anaphase I separates homologs into egg and first polar body; anaphase II splits the egg's sisters.
cards.quote: Anaphase I kept the A homolog, with its two A sisters, in the egg and sent the a homolog into the first polar body.
cards.section: Four sperm, one egg

cards.front: Cohesin links sister chromatids from S phase. How do sisters stay joined after anaphase I until anaphase II?
cards.back: Arm cohesin is cut at anaphase I, but cohesin around the centromeres is protected by shugoshin until anaphase II (in yeast and mammals as studied).
cards.quote: cohesin around the centromeres is protected by a protein called shugoshin until anaphase II
cards.section: Four sperm, one egg

cards.front: In an oocyte, cohesin on the chromosome arms is made uncleavable, while everything else runs on schedule. Predict what happens at anaphase I, and why.
cards.back: In most organisms studied, homologs fail to separate at anaphase I. A crossover plus the arm cohesion beyond it holds homologs together; with that cohesion uncut, the spindle cannot pull them to opposite poles.
cards.why: Rests on the lesson's rule that cutting arm cohesin is what releases homologs (in most organisms studied).
cards.quote: Its link, a crossover plus the cohesion beyond it holding homologs together until anaphase I so the spindle can pull them to opposite poles
cards.section: Crossing over: what holds the pair, and what it does to alleles

cards.front: In an Aa cell, one crossover falls between the A locus and its centromere. At which division do A and a part, and why?
cards.back: Anaphase II. The crossover swaps the A-locus segment between one chromatid of each homolog, so each homolog leaves meiosis I with one A and one a chromatid.
cards.why: Sisters are no longer identical at A, so they part at anaphase II. Each product still gets one allele.
cards.quote: So each homolog leaves meiosis I carrying one A chromatid and one a chromatid.
cards.section: Crossing over: what holds the pair, and what it does to alleles

cards.front: A female fly is Aa Bb, A and B on different chromosomes. One crossover falls between A and its centromere, none near B. How many kinds of gamete can this one meiosis give?
cards.back: Four kinds, one each of AB, aB, Ab and ab. B and b part at anaphase I; each resulting cell then splits A from a at anaphase II.
cards.why: Pooled over many meioses the ratio is still 1:1:1:1.
cards.quote: So one meiosis gives AB, aB, Ab and ab.
cards.section: Crossing over: what holds the pair, and what it does to alleles

cards.front: What does an ordinary crossover change about segregation at a locus, and what does it not change?
cards.back: It can change when A and a part (anaphase II instead of I). It does not change the deal: each gamete gets one allele, two A and two a.
cards.quote: A crossover does not change the deal: each gamete still gets one allele, and an ordinary crossover leaves two A and two a.
cards.section: Crossing over: what holds the pair, and what it does to alleles

cards.front: Name the five substages of prophase I in order.
cards.back: Leptotene, zygotene, pachytene, diplotene, diakinesis.
cards.quote: cytologists divide it into substages by how the chromosomes look
cards.section: Crossing over: what holds the pair, and what it does to alleles

cards.front: In pachytene, homologs are fully synapsed, held by the {{c1::synaptonemal complex}}, a protein structure that zips them together along their length.
cards.back: Crossing over is completed here.
cards.quote: Pachytene: homologs are fully synapsed, held by the synaptonemal complex, a protein structure that zips them together along their length.
cards.section: Crossing over: what holds the pair, and what it does to alleles

cards.front: After the synaptonemal complex comes apart in diplotene, homologs stay joined at {{c1::chiasmata}}, the visible sites of earlier crossovers.
cards.back: Singular: chiasma.
cards.quote: they stay joined at chiasmata (singular chiasma), the visible sites of earlier crossovers
cards.section: Crossing over: what holds the pair, and what it does to alleles

cards.front: What did Sutton argue from grasshopper chromosomes, and why did it remain a hypothesis?
cards.back: Maternal and paternal members pair, then separate, each pair orienting independently, predicting both of Mendel's laws. He could not tell maternal from paternal members in his material.
cards.quote: He saw that they came in matched pairs, and in 1903 argued that maternal and paternal members pair and then separate, each pair orienting independently.
cards.section: Sutton, Boveri and the proof

cards.front: In sea urchin eggs fertilized by two sperm, chromosomes were distributed unevenly among three or four poles, and the resulting cells as a rule developed abnormally. What did Boveri conclude?
cards.back: Development needs a particular combination of chromosomes, not merely a number, so different chromosomes carry different things.
cards.quote: He concluded that development needs a particular combination of chromosomes, not merely a number, so different chromosomes carry different things.
cards.section: Sutton, Boveri and the proof

cards.front: How did Carothers' grasshopper males let her test independent orientation directly, and what did she find?
cards.back: One pair was heteromorphic (one member visibly larger) and the X was unpaired, so she could see which homolog the X went with. It went with each about equally often.
cards.quote: In grasshopper males with one heteromorphic pair, meaning one member visibly larger, and an unpaired X, she could see which homolog the X travelled with.
cards.section: Sutton, Boveri and the proof

cards.front: In 300 first meiotic divisions, an unpaired X goes with the larger homolog of a heteromorphic pair 165 times and with the smaller 135 times. Compute χ² and decide whether the counts fit independent orientation (critical value 3.84, 1 df, P = 0.05).
cards.back: Expected 150 and 150. χ² = 15^2/150 + 15^2/150 = 450/150 = 3.0. Below 3.84, so consistent with independent orientation.
cards.quote: With two classes there is 1 degree of freedom, and the critical value at P = 0.05 is 3.84.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: In the same kind of grasshopper study, what would evidence of dependent orientation look like? Compute χ² for 220 versus 80 out of 300.
cards.back: χ² = 70^2/150 + 70^2/150 = 65.3, far above 3.84. Dependence would be a large excess in one direction like this that recurs in other males and preparations.
cards.why: One small deviation is what sampling noise produces, though it cannot rule out a small real bias.
cards.quote: A large excess in one direction, for example 220 to 80 (χ² = 65.3), that recurs in other males and preparations.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: A study finds that an unpaired X and a heteromorphic pair orient independently at meiosis I. What does this support, and what does it not show by itself?
cards.back: It shows, by sight, that two non-homologous chromosomes assort as Mendel's second law needs if genes sit on chromosomes. It does not show that any gene is on these chromosomes.
cards.quote: It does not by itself show that any gene is on these chromosomes.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Two crossovers fall between locus A and its centromere, both between the same two chromatids (a two-strand double). At which division do A and a part? What if it is a three-strand double?
cards.back: Two-strand: anaphase I, because the second exchange swaps the segment back and the sisters match again. Three-strand: anaphase II, because the sisters stay different.
cards.quote: Either way the sisters match again, and A and a part at anaphase I.
cards.section: When a crossover does not move the split

cards.front: How can one meiosis in an Aa cell give three A and one a?
cards.back: Gene conversion: the break repair that makes crossovers can copy a short stretch of one homolog onto a chromatid of the other, so a locus inside that stretch can give 3:1.
cards.quote: At a locus inside such a stretch, one meiosis can give three A and one a.
cards.section: When the count is not two and two
